# Disagreement Log — 1 Maccabees Chapter 3

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Translators:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA

---

## Summary
Total disagreements: 35

---

## Disagreement Entries

**1MA 3:3 — "put on a breastplate like a giant"**
- EMET/LOGOS: "put on a breastplate like a giant"
- PNEUMA: "strapped on armor like a giant"
- RULING: "put on a breastplate like a giant" — *enedusato thoraka* is specifically a breastplate, not generic armor

**1MA 3:3 — "set battles in order" vs. "set his battle lines"**
- EMET: "set battles in order"
- LOGOS: "Set battles in order"
- PNEUMA: "set his battle lines"
- RULING: "set battles in order" — the Greek *parataxeis* refers to the marshaling of forces; "battle lines" is acceptable but "set in order" is more literal

**1MA 3:4 — "lion's cub" vs. "young lion"**
- EMET: "lion's cub"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "young lion"
- RULING: "young lion" — *skumnos leontos* is a lion cub or young lion; "young lion" is more evocative in English and matches the Genesis 49 echo

**1MA 3:5 — "burned with fire those who troubled" vs. "burned those who troubled"**
- EMET: "burned with fire"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "burned those who"
- RULING: "burned those who troubled his people" — the metaphorical use of "burned" covers both readings; adding "with fire" is redundant

**1MA 3:6 — "salvation was prospered in his hand" vs. "deliverance prospered by his hand"**
- EMET: "salvation was prospered in his hand"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "deliverance prospered by his hand"
- RULING: "deliverance prospered by his hand" — EMET's "salvation" imports theological freight not intended here; this is military deliverance

**1MA 3:7 — "embittered many kings" vs. "brought grief to many kings"**
- EMET: "embittered many kings"
- LOGOS: "brought grief to many kings"
- PNEUMA: "made kings bitter"
- RULING: "brought grief to many kings" — *epikranen* can mean both "embittered" and "brought grief/pain to"; in context of defeat, "grief" is better

**1MA 3:8 — "destroyed the ungodly out of them" vs. "destroying the ungodly from among them"**
- EMET: "destroyed the ungodly out of them"
- LOGOS: "destroying the ungodly from among them"
- RULING: "destroying the ungodly from among them" — LOGOS preposition is more natural

**1MA 3:10 — "gathered the nations" vs. "gathered together the Gentiles"**
- EMET: "gathered the nations"
- LOGOS: "gathered together the Gentiles"
- PNEUMA: "mustered the Gentiles"
- RULING: "gathered the Gentiles" — standard rendering; "mustered" (PNEUMA) is good but "gathered" is more neutral

**1MA 3:12 — "with it he fought all his days"**
- All translators agree. This is a memorable detail all preserve. No disagreement.

**1MA 3:13 — "assembly of faithful men and a congregation"**
- EMET: "assembly of faithful men and a congregation with him"
- LOGOS: "a company of faithful men...a congregation ready for war"
- PNEUMA: "a fighting force — faithful men who stood with him"
- RULING: "a company of faithful men with him, a congregation" — the double designation (*athroisma...synagoge*) should be preserved; both terms have communal/religious weight

**1MA 3:14 — "disregarded the command" vs. "defied the command"**
- EMET: "disregarded the command"
- LOGOS: "defied the king's command"
- PNEUMA: "spit on the king's command"
- RULING: "defied the king's command" — active defiance rather than passive disregard

**1MA 3:16 — "a small company" vs. "a small band of men"**
- EMET/LOGOS: "a small company"
- PNEUMA: "only a small band of men"
- RULING: "a small company" — simple and direct

**1MA 3:17 — "so great and strong a multitude" vs. "such a great and powerful multitude"**
- EMET: "so great and strong a multitude"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "such a great and powerful multitude"
- RULING: "such a great and powerful multitude" — LOGOS formulation is more natural

**1MA 3:18 — "shut up in the hands of a few" vs. "hemmed in by few"**
- EMET: "shut up in the hands of a few"
- LOGOS: "hemmed in by few"
- PNEUMA: "trapped by few"
- RULING: "hemmed in by few" — LOGOS captures the military encirclement (*sunklisai*) well

**1MA 3:19 — "Victory in battle" opening**
- All translators agree on the theological assertion. Minor word variation only.
- RULING: "Victory in war does not depend on the size of the fighting force; strength comes from Heaven."

**1MA 3:22 — "he himself will crush them" — subject of "he"**
- EMET: "he himself will crush them"
- LOGOS: "God himself will crush them"
- PNEUMA: "God himself will shatter them"
- RULING: "he himself will crush them" — the Greek *autos* is simply "he/himself"; making it explicit as "God" is an interpretive addition, though contextually obvious; EMET's ambiguity mirrors the original

**1MA 3:23 — "fell upon them suddenly" vs. "charged them suddenly" vs. "Suddenly"**
- EMET: "fell upon them suddenly"
- LOGOS: "charged them suddenly"
- PNEUMA: "charged. Suddenly."
- RULING: "charged them suddenly" — clear and direct

**1MA 3:25 — "fame reached the king" vs. "fame spread to the king"**
- Minor variation. "His fame reached the king" (LOGOS) is preferred.

**1MA 3:26 — "angry in his soul" vs. "filled with rage"**
- EMET: "angry in his soul"
- LOGOS: "filled with rage"
- PNEUMA: "erupted in fury"
- RULING: "was filled with rage" — LOGOS; "angry in his soul" is literal but awkward; "erupted" is too dramatic

**1MA 3:28 — "plague which he had made" vs. "ruin he had brought upon"**
- EMET: "plague which he had made"
- LOGOS: "disaster he had brought"
- PNEUMA: "disorder he himself had created"
- RULING: "ruin he had brought upon the land" — *pleges* means a wound/strike/plague; "ruin" captures the lasting damage better than "disaster"

**1MA 3:29 — "more lavishly than the kings before him" vs. "above the kings who were before him"**
- EMET: "above the kings who were before him"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "more lavishly than the kings before him" / "outspending every king before him"
- RULING: "more lavishly than the kings before him" — the comparison of his spending is the point

**1MA 3:31 — "from the river Euphrates" vs. "from the Euphrates River"**
- Minor stylistic variation. "From the Euphrates River to the borders of Egypt" (LOGOS) adopted.

**1MA 3:34 — "crush and root out" vs. "crush and uproot"**
- EMET: "crush and root out"
- LOGOS: "crush and uproot"
- RULING: "crush and uproot" — "uproot" is more natural English

**1MA 3:34 — "take away their memorial" vs. "blot out their memory"**
- EMET: "take away their memorial from that place"
- LOGOS: "blot out their memory from that place"
- PNEUMA: "erase their memory from that place"
- RULING: "blot out their very memory from that place" — *exarai to mnemosynon* means to remove/destroy the very record of their existence; "blot out" is vivid and appropriate

**1MA 3:39 — "plain country" vs. "coastal plain"**
- EMET: "plain country"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "coastal plain"
- RULING: "coastal plain" — the Shephelah/Emmaus area is the Judean foothills/coastal plain; "coastal plain" is more geographically precise

**1MA 3:40 — "fetters" — explanation needed?**
- All translators preserve "fetters" (chains for slaves). No disagreement; the word is self-explanatory in context.

**1MA 3:41 — "evils were multiplied" vs. "situation was growing desperate"**
- EMET: "evils were multiplied"
- LOGOS: "situation was growing desperate"
- PNEUMA: "crisis was deepening"
- RULING: "their situation was growing desperate" — LOGOS captures the sense of the deteriorating situation; EMET is more literal but "evils were multiplied" is awkward

**1MA 3:42 — "raise up the ruin" vs. "restore the ruins" vs. "rebuild what has been ruined"**
- EMET: "raise up the ruin of our people"
- LOGOS: "restore our people from their ruin"
- PNEUMA: "rebuild what has been ruined"
- RULING: "restore the ruins of our people" — LOGOS; the verbal form *anastesai* is "to raise up/restore"

**1MA 3:44 — "pipe and the harp had ceased" vs. "pipe and harp had fallen silent"**
- EMET: "pipe and the harp had ceased"
- LOGOS: "pipe and harp had fallen silent"
- PNEUMA: "the music had stopped"
- RULING: "pipe and harp had fallen silent" — LOGOS; preserves the specific instruments; "fallen silent" is evocative

**1MA 3:47 — "paint likenesses of their idols" vs. "likenesses for their idols"**
- EMET: "paint likenesses of their idols"
- LOGOS: "patterns for painting the likenesses of their idols"
- RULING: "paint the likenesses of their idols" — the Torah scrolls had been defaced by being used as drawing patterns for idol images; LOGOS's expansion is explanatory but acceptable

**1MA 3:52 — "how shall we be able to stand" vs. "how will we be able to stand"**
- Minor tense variation. No substantive disagreement.

**1MA 3:54 — Military organization terms**
- All translators agree on "commanders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens" — this echoes Exodus 18 (Jethro's advice) deliberately. No disagreement.

**1MA 3:55 — "according to the Torah"**
- All translators preserve this legal reference to Deuteronomy 20:5-8 (exemptions from military service). No disagreement.

**1MA 3:57 — "be men of valor" vs. "be brave men" vs. "be soldiers"**
- EMET: "be men of valor"
- LOGOS: "be brave men"
- PNEUMA: "be soldiers"
- RULING: "be valiant" — *andreizesthe* means "play the man/be courageous"; "valiant" is concise

**1MA 3:59 — "as the will of Heaven is, so shall he do" vs. "whatever the will of Heaven may be"**
- EMET: "as the will of Heaven is, so shall he do"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "whatever the will of Heaven may be, so shall it be done"
- RULING: "whatever the will of Heaven may be — so shall it be done" — the impersonal construction avoids ambiguity over the subject
